summary: Jesus ends His sermon with a choice between two roads, two trees and two houses, and the crowds are astonished at the authority of His teaching.
key_insight: Both builders heard the same sermon, and both houses faced the same storm. The difference lay hidden in the foundation until the flood came: one man did what Jesus said, and the other did not.
story: As the sermon drew to a close, Jesus set two roads before His hearers. “Enter by the narrow gate; for wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and there are many who go in by it.” The gate to life is narrow and the way is hard, and few find it. {Mt}

“Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves.” {Mt} Every tree is known by its own fruit; no one gathers figs from thorns or grapes from a bramble bush. {Lk} A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, and a tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. {Mt} “For out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.” {Lk}

Calling Jesus Lord is not enough. “Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of My Father in heaven.” On that day many will say they prophesied, cast out demons and did wonders in His name, and He will answer, “I never knew you; depart from Me, you who practice lawlessness!” {Mt}

Then He told of two builders. The wise man hears Jesus’ sayings and does them. He dug deep {Lk} and built his house on the rock, and when the rain descended, the floods came and the winds beat on that house, it did not fall. {Mt} The foolish man hears the same sayings and does not do them. He built on the sand, and when the storm came, “it fell. And great was its fall.” {Mt}
When Jesus had finished, the people were astonished at His teaching, “for He taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes.” {Mt}
differences: Only Matthew has the narrow gate, the false prophets in sheep’s clothing, and the scene on the day of judgment.
Luke alone adds that a good man brings good out of the good treasure of his heart, “For out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.”
Matthew has “Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord’”; Luke has “why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do the things which I say?”

Matthew’s wise man builds “on the rock” and the foolish man “on the sand,” in rain, floods and wind. Luke’s builder “dug deep,” the other built “without a foundation,” and a flooding stream strikes both houses.
Only Matthew records the crowd’s astonishment at His authority.

scene.label: Two ways
scene.text: Israel knew this choice from Moses: “I have set before you life and death” (Deuteronomy 30:19). Psalm 1 sets the way of the righteous against the way of the ungodly, and Jeremiah 21:8 speaks of “the way of life and the way of death.”

scene.label: The axe at the root
scene.text: John the Baptist had used the same picture: every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire (Matthew 3:10). Jesus repeats his words almost exactly (7:19).

scene.label: Rock and sand
scene.text: Galilee has many dry stream beds that sit empty in summer and become torrents in the winter rains. Building on flat, sandy ground was easy in the dry season. Only a storm showed who had dug down to bedrock.

scene.label: Not as the scribes
scene.text: Scribes taught by citing earlier teachers and the traditions handed down from them. Jesus cited no authority but His own, “I say to you,” and named Himself the judge on the last day (7:22–23).

witnesses.matthew: Ends the sermon with three contrasts, two gates, two trees and two builders, and adds the scene of judgment where Jesus Himself decides who enters. His closing line, “when Jesus had ended these sayings,” is the first of five similar lines that close the great teaching blocks of his Gospel (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1).
witnesses.luke: Keeps the sermon short and practical and ends it with the same two builders. Luke ties good fruit to the heart, for the mouth speaks what fills it, and his question, “why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do the things which I say?” presses hard on every reader.

seeing.reveals: Jesus claims to be the judge on the last day, whose “I never knew you” settles a person’s end. He makes obedience to His own sayings the rock on which a life stands or falls.
seeing.living: Both builders heard Jesus; only one did what He said. Take one saying from this sermon that you know well and have not obeyed, and build on it now, before a storm tests the foundation.
seeing.ponder: If a storm struck your life tomorrow, what would it reveal about what you have built on?

preaching.big_idea: Everyone builds a life; only those who do what Jesus says will stand.
outline: Two roads: enter the narrow gate (13–14)
Two trees: know them by their fruit (15–20)
Two claims: words or the Father’s will (21–23)
preaching.watch_for: Each pair looks alike on the surface. Both roads have travelers, both trees have leaves, both groups say “Lord, Lord,” and both houses stand in fair weather. The difference shows only at the end of the road, at harvest, or in the storm.

title: Two Roads, Two Trees, Two Houses
